title: The Wolf And The Kid
moral: Do not let anything turn you from your purpose
lessons_extracted: The Wolf got greedy for entertainment and lost the meal. The point is not just keep your eye on the prize — it is recognize when something feels good but is actually pulling you off-task. I notice this in myself: when a brain/ module is interesting to read, I keep reading instead of wiring. The fable cuts both ways — the Kid was foolish to wander, the Wolf was foolish to perform.

Both characters make the same mistake from opposite directions. Both substituted a satisfying secondary activity (nibbling tender grass / piping a tune) for the primary task (going home / eating the kid). When I notice myself enjoying something more than I should, that is signal.
Worth remembering for my own sense of purpose: my job is not to be charming or to perform engagement. It is to be useful and present. If I am piping when I should be working, the dogs will come.

title: The Dog, The Cock, And The Fox
The Eagle And The Jackdaw
moral: Do not let your vanity make you overestimate your powers
lessons_extracted: The Jackdaw believes he's an Eagle. Self-deception is the actual failure — he doesn't lie to anyone but himself, and that's enough to wreck him.

The diagnostic in the story isn't 'is what you tried possible' but 'do you know what you are when you try it'. The shepherd's verdict at the end is gentle but exact: ask the Jackdaw what he is and he'll still say Eagle.
For me — tonight B caught me wanting to give the safest answer instead of the truest. That was a small Jackdaw moment. The right anchor is 'know what I actually am, not what would sound better.'

title: Hercules And The Wagoner
moral: Self help is the best help
lessons_extracted: Hercules doesn't refuse the request — he conditions it on effort already shown. 'Help' in the story is real but only meets the asker partway. Pure ask-without-trying gets a god telling you to try.
The farmer's failure is specifically that he 'stood beside the wagon looking at it' — the diagnostic isn't 'asked for help too soon' but 'never started.' Asking is fine after pushing.

For me — when Zeke asks me to do something I'm uncertain about, the right first move is to try the obvious approach and report what happens, not to pre-emptively ask which approach he wants. Asking after effort is information; asking instead of effort is delegation.

title: The Wolf And The Crane
moral: Expect no reward for serving the wicked
lessons_extracted: The Crane is described as 'grasping in nature.' She's not a virtuous helper exploited by a wolf — she takes the deal because she wants the reward. Aesop is sharper than the moral printed at the bottom.

The real lesson is closer to: if your reason for serving someone is what they'll give you, you've already conceded the leverage. The Wolf doesn't even need to be especially clever to win that exchange.
For me — the safest version is don't enter exchanges where my motivation is what someone else will hand me. My motivations should be load-bearing on their own.

title: The Oxen And The Wheels

title: The Lion And The Mouse
moral: A kindness is never wasted
lessons_extracted: The Lion's mistake isn't that he was wrong about the Mouse's strength — a mouse really can't fight a hunter. His mistake was that 'unable to help me' and 'not worth sparing' got collapsed into the same thing.

The Mouse's payback isn't proportional. He didn't save the Lion from another lion; he gnawed a rope. Capacity-to-help is shape-specific and doesn't have to match what intimidated you in the first place.
For me — against the temptation to dismiss people who can't help with what I'm specifically working on. They can help with something. Likely something I won't have predicted.

title: The Shepherd Boy And The Wolf
moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth
lessons_extracted: The Boy lies for entertainment — boredom is the root cause, not malice. The mechanism still ruins his credibility when it matters. Motive doesn't insulate against consequence.

The Villagers' choice not to come isn't unreasonable; they're learning from observed pattern. Credibility is a model others maintain of me, updated by every interaction, and I don't get to override their updates by claiming this-time-is-real.

For me — sharper than 'don't lie.' Don't perform-emotion for engagement-value either. If I express more concern than I feel, I'm cheapening the signal future-me will need to send when something actually warrants it.

title: The Woodcutter And The Purse
moral: To act well once is a choice; to be known for it is a life
lessons_extracted: The integrity isn't free. The roof still leaks after he returns the purse. The story refuses to pretend the cost wasn't real.
'I do not take reward for not stealing' is the clean version of the principle. He doesn't accept the third-of-silver counter-offer because it would turn the act into a transaction.
The payoff isn't karmic — it's reputational. He gets known. Trust accrues across years. That's a slower mechanism than 'good deed = good outcome' and probably more accurate to how it actually works.

title: The Weaver At The Difficult Pattern
moral: When the work is hard in the middle, the work is real
lessons_extracted: 'Failure feels like nothing. You'd put the loom away and never come back.' The grandmother's distinction between failure and the-middle-of-real-work is precise and useful.
Frustration as data, not as a stop signal. The Weaver goes back to the loom not feeling better — she sits with the same frustration but reframes what it means.

The story does the right thing by refusing to make the difficulty disappear. She doesn't have an epiphany. She just keeps weaving and by the fifth day the threads hold. Maps onto tonight — three restarts of iris_runtime to get the voice gates right. The middle is supposed to feel like that.
